editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: The first thing we like to do to start is just have you tell us your name and spell your last name for us.

sp.speaker: Mathew William Gundersen
sp.p: Okay. My name is Matt Gundersen, Mathew, and my last name is spelled G-U-N-D-E-R-S-E-N. I'm a Norwegian. And I joined the Navy the day after World War II started, and I went to this -- they give me a week off to get things squared away, and the 17th I left for San Diego for boot camp. And I was in boot camp a week gettin' my shots and that, and that's about all -- they give us a wooden rifle to learn the manual arms, but that's about it. Went to San Francisco and they got on a tug and went over to the ship I was going to, the Hammondsport CV2, and they were over Alameda loading planes. And I went aboard there, and the first thing, I was on deck. I was a seaman. And I stood watches on the pier, and that was the coldest watches I ever had in my life 'cause it was rainin' and cold. In them days, you didn't have anything -- I had a pea coat on, but you'd get soakin' wet on one four-hour watch. When I went aboard, they asked me where I wanted to be, and, of course, in high school I took a machine shop course. I was -- and I had a year-and-a-half off my apprenticeship, so I told them engine room. And I was still put on deck but they took me down and put me in the engineering department. And I was educated by Asiatic sailors that -- smartest guys I ever met, and they stared at the ceiling while they talked to you, and they were finest bunch you ever meet. Well, while I was on deck, I stood gun watches, crows nest watches, but when I got off watch, I was down in the fire room tracin' lines, learning how to light off pumps and I'd stand watch on the boiler. And over in the engine room I'm learning all -- all the pumps. And they got me down in the fire -- fire room early. There was about 15 guys ahead of me on the list waitin' to get into the fire room but because of my machinist experience, they took me down below. Well, when I was in the fire room, I could stand watches immediately 'cause I learned how while I was still on deck. But all my work was in the machine shop. They -- they immediately put me in the machine shop where I did all the machine work for valves and stuff. Most of the machine was all reciprocating, so I'd have to make rings and that thing and your sliding valves and things like that. And we loaded -- the planes were loaded and we left San Francisco and we was headed for Manila and halfway there Manila fell, so we went to Brisbane, Australia. And we got in -- Brisbane, Australia is 60 miles up the river in Australia there, and there was no pier, there was just a mole. We tied up to the mole. And they had an old donkey steam boiler -- boiler on the beach for handling the fuel lines and stuff and handling the planes. We took -- took and unloaded our planes. And, in fact, what we carried, we carried a Marine detachment; pilots, mechanics, the whole works. In fact, when they got to Brisbane, four hours after we was there, they had a P-40 in the air. That's how good they were. And going ashore we had a couple planks that you had to walk the plank about 50 feet, and that was an experience in itself. And we had one guy on the ship, he came back with a horse after liberty. But they're -- they're the most friendly people in the world, the Australians. Of course, all the Australian men were already in North Africa. They -- England stripped them first. They called them up first, you know. So people would stop us on the street and say, "Hey, Yank, come on out to the house and listen to the wireless." And they'd have a daughter for -- for you to meet, you know. They were very gracious. And the bars were hotels and they closed at 5:00 and then opened at 8 again. But that would be from 5 to 8, if you went to a restaurant, you could get something to eat and drink and have a drink there. But it was very good. And when we left Australia, we went through New Zealand. We hit a typhoon, and we had an albatross that followed us for about six, seven days. I mean just coastin' over the ship. He didn't -- wouldn't flap a wing once, just the air currents, just coasted along with us. And of course I was in the crows nest watchin' him a lot. And we -- we thought we was goin' to Valparaiso, Chile, 'cause we headed straight for Valparaiso after we went through New Zealand, straits of New Zealand there. And we got over to the parallel, straight up to San Francisco. So we turned north and we got off Panama and a cruiser fired a shot off over our bow, our cruiser, because we only had -- the only officers on the -- on the ship was a captain and the chief engineer. There was all the -- all the rest were civilian and merchant marine. And they had a chief signalman that wasn't on the bridge at the time, they had to get him up there to get the blaker (ph) open to cut the canvas open so he could answer. That's the thing. Called, you know, to this cruiser. And after about ten minutes they got squared away on that. And we went on to San Francisco and we was in San Francisco three days, we loaded up with planes and we headed for Pearl. Now, we went into Pearl and we off -- off loaded our planes at Ford Island and we left Pearl and we went -- went out to Johnson Island. And Johnson Island is about 700 miles from Pearl. And we off loaded aviation gas in barrels. And the water was so shallow that the natives would come out and we'd just drop the barrels on out and they'd push them ashore. And it -- it was very, very interesting watching. And then we went back to the States. The most we'd be in the States would be three days, just to off load the wrecked planes that we'd pick up. And then we headed for Noumea, New Caledonia. And we always traveled solo, nobody -- with no escort. Staging place was Noumea Cal -- Caledonia. They had a repair ship there, and that's -- if there was a carrier in there, we'd put planes aboard there and take their wrecks, but if not, we'd take and pick up an escort. The Runner was the most -- the Australian destroyer, the Runner, was mostly our escort. And we'd go into Guadalcanal and we had to be in there 8:30 in the morning and leave at 3:30, and then we'd zigzag all night and then go back there the next day. We had our own barcas aboard with great big Johnson Evinrude engines on it to run the barges back and forth to the beach. And it was an all hands evolution. There was no stevedores or anything. We were the stevedores. The crew did everything. Everything was all hands. And then we -- we'd be in there for maybe two days -- one day to unload, the next day to pick up the wrecks, then we'd go back to the States. The Runner would escort us for a day and then leave us and we was on our -- on our way back to the States again. And we'd go into either San Diego or San Francisco and load up, then we'd head for Pearl. We'd go into Pearl. We -- when the torpedo squadron that was lost in -- in Midway, we off loaded them on a Jeep carrier in Pearl Harbor. And then we -- we went into Dole Pineapple dock and we had cement, and we unloaded cement on -- for them. And I didn't -- I didn't mention but, you know, when we left Brisbane, we brought back a load of wool. And when a typhoon, that -- that wool started to shift, the bales of wool, and there was an all hands evol -- evolution down on the deck. See, the ship had an elevator right in the center of the ship and could go down three decks. And each one of them decks had railroad cars because before the war it was a sea train Nevada (ph), and all these decks was just loaded with wool. I mean, there was a lot of wool. And we was down there baling, you know, shifting the bale and proppin' it up and what have you. Then we'd get back to the States and we'd load up again, get rid of our damaged planes and off again we'd go. And we'd get to Pearl and -- we'd go to Pearl and then we'd take and go down to Pago Pago and Futa Futi (ph), in that area, and off load our -- not planes but other materials, you know. And we carried a lot of fuel and a lot of water, and the small crafts, they didn't have the ability to make enough water for the crew half the time, so we -- we had plenty of water in our vats, kept us up full so that we -- we'd transfer water mostly to just about anybody. And then -- then we'd head back to the States. And, of course, when I got in the fire room, bein' -- bein' a machinist, I took over the machine shop. I did all the work in the machine shop. And after -- four months after I was in, I made seaman second. And a month later I was down in the fire room and I made fireman first, which is the same as third class, and then four months later I made second class, because I was doin' the work in the machine shop and that. And in order to make first class, I had to stand engine room watches. Well, during my pre-training by the Asiatics, they -- I didn't know it at the time, this guy I hated with -- oh, I wanted to get him on the beach and beat him up because -- because he would challenge me on everything. He -- "What kind of a sailor are you? Are you a sailor or a seaman?" You know, and he'd challenge me. "Are you a fireman or a fireman first?" You know, on everything. Every day I wanted to get him on the beach. He turned out to be one of my best friends. In fact, there -- James Junior Dow (ph) and Henry Charles Nothin (ph) became my mentors. And every day he would put up a message on -- on the bulletin board for the brains. And we had class. We had a chief warrant that held school on us that -- that on the fact we'd get back there and we -- we had the naval machinery and we -- we knew that naval machinery inside and out because he questioned us on everything. And I -- I by being in the machine shop, doing all the work on -- on the reciprocating pumps and things like making rings and what have you, I was pretty well _____. The three of us, we decided if the ship was hit, it would split in half, right -- because they had the big elevator deck right in the center of the ship. Well, the engine room and everything was aft. And we practiced isolating the aft part of the ship from the rest of the ship, the tanks and what have you. And we was gonna baton down the ship. We -- when they say abandon ship, we was gonna stay aboard. And we practiced like -- like we was gonna close this valve and that valve, and we'd -- we'd take and practice every chance we got. 'Cause we -- we knew we was gonna get that, we was gonna save that ship. We was gonna claim survivor, you know. But we -- we had a real good time doin' it. And it was back and forth. And first -- we made three trips in the Guadalcanal and the last trip there, we got to go over to -- they have a volcano with a lake in it carved out and swim and you could -- branches of trees, you can hang on the trees and swing out and dive in. And that was great. That was a great recreation. We went to Bougainville and then -- but mostly went to Pearl and then offsprings to that but I -- of course, I'm a young kid and I'm eager to get in the real Navy, so to speak, 'cause all -- all these Asiatics, they were saying -- saying, "You ought to be in the real Navy." You know. Or "Are you a sailor?" Every -- Charles Nothin (ph) -- we called him Blacky Stacks. And old Blacky would say, you -- "Are you a sailor or just a civilian in a sailor's suit?" You know. He ribbed me all the time. And we finished up. I got back to the States in '43. I got -- got to get transferred for new construction, and I went to -- right up here at Puget Sound Naval Shipyard, and the loyds (ph) -- we call it the Leutze, DD 481, it was a Fletcher-class destroyer. And --

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Before we go to the Leutze, let's talk a little bit more about Hammondsport. Could you take me on it and just kind of describe the ship to us? What it looked like, what kind of weaponry it had, et cetera?

sp.speaker: Mathew William Gundersen
sp.p: Well, it looked like a box, and right in the center of it, I'd say about 50 feet -- the ship was actually about 35 feet wide and this well in the center was just like where the elevator went down. You could put four planes with the wings floated back on that elevator and go down. And then it had the -- the bridge forward, and the engine room and everything was back aft. And it -- it was -- it drew 35 feet of water and it -- to the main deck was 50 feet from the bottom of the hold, 50 feet high. And -- 'cause that was an awful light of plane. In them days you didn't have dungarees. When you was over the side, you was either in whites, undressed whites, or undressed blues. And when I was on the deck, I didn't get any dungarees until I was in the fire room. And then when in the fire room, we had to change clothes before we left the fire room and put on the uniform of the day to go up topside to go to meal. To go eat, you had to be in the uniform of the day. You know, they -- they had -- everybody was really in order. You know, you know what you did and you did it right. And it was -- our speed was 16.618, day in and day out. You know, and, actually, two men could stand the watches and run the evap -- evaporators at the same time. In fact, the DA tank, the aerating and feed tank in the engine room was -- reciprocating engine pump was -- would regulate the water level in that, and the water level in that, the right level was the same level in the boilers. So you had a steam valve that, as the water rose and lowered, would allow more steam or cut off the steam for pumping the water into the DA tank. So you maintained that. Then from the platform of the engine room you could see everything in the fire room, see, all the pressures and everything. You had your gauges on your throttle board anyhow. So -- and the evaps were in the back and up. And the generator was a pressure. It carried 50 -- 15 pounds of back pressure. It didn't have a -- a cooler, you know. Didn't run under a vacuum, it run under pressure. And it worked good. You worried about it sometime, you know, if it got -- really fell if the pressure got too high. But -- and all the drains went in the hot well. See, the generator would exhaust into the exhaust line that goes to the DA tank and all drains went in the hot well. You had an open hot well, and then you had a pump that pumped the water up from the hot well up to the DA tank. It was -- it was really nice. One school, big school, but it took us --

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Was it pretty noisy in the engine room?

sp.speaker: Mathew William Gundersen
sp.p: Well, you get used to noise. You don't know what noise is anymore, you know. I know one thing that you learn, when there's a different sound, you immediately know what to do, you know. I mean, if there's a different sound, you know something's wrong. Now, we had natural ventilation. We didn't have exhaust blowers or anything like that, we had funnels that went to topside with -- that furnished our air. And that's -- you could find anybody on lone watch, he was standin' under a ventilator. And you'd take -- now, when I got in the fire room, my -- because I was in the machine shop all the time doing work, I didn't have time to work much in the fire room, so they made me the assistant oil thing. That way I learned all the tanks on the ship. And I had a chief that -- the chief -- now, this chief was afraid to come down to the fire room because the Asiatics were, you know, top watches. And nothing -- nothing was a second class. And I didn't know it at the time, but he only spoke to two people on the ship and that was the captain and the -- and the chief engineer. And, of course, he spoke to James Junior Dow (ph) and me, and I didn't know that I was -- he liked me but it took me a long time to discover it. But the three of us, we really worked good together. And he was still second class when I made second class and he was still second class when I made first class because he -- all -- he was mad, he had a couple -- he had a Chinese wife and a couple Chinese children, and he always -- always say make -- they were good communists, you know.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Now, you joined the day after Pearl Harbor --

sp.speaker: Mathew William Gundersen
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: -- I'm guessing. Tell me why you joined.

sp.speaker: Mathew William Gundersen
sp.p: Well, that -- that was the only thing to do. I was a young kid, full of pep and vinegar, you know. I worked all my life. I was raised on a dairy and my dad was a nice man and my grandpa was a nice man, and they cut ice off the lakes and they had -- my grandfather had 23 ice houses at one time, artificial ice -- no artificial, you know, they -- from the river and from the lakes. And so I -- I grew up workin'. And my junior year in high school, I went to work for Consolidated Machinery and Supply Company and what we was doin' was, they'd go out into a farmer that had his own shop, maybe in the basement, maybe in the shed, they'd buy it up and they'd bring it in the shop and I -- I was the guy to restore it. We'd tear it all apart and dip it. And while I was there -- we had three automatics goin'. You know, remember when -- the day they made spark plugs with the two parts, with the -- well, we made 500,000 of them spark plug. You know, we had three -- three automatics, Cleveland automatics, runnin' 24 hours a day. I'd go to work at 1:00 and I'd work till 6:00 at night, and that's when I was a junior in high school. Or maybe 7. Then my boss' wife would come and she'd work from 6:00 till midnight. And my boss was a -- a projector, he ran the projector down at the Orpheum Theater and -- and he'd take over at midnight from his wife and work till 8:00 in the morning, and then she'd come back and work from 8:00 in the morning till _____. And usually -- Alex was my boss. Either he or I would -- would set up the heads for the automatic. So all she had to do -- you check these with no, no good gauges, and when you got thin, you'd put a 20-foot piece of material in it and let it go. And when -- the bell would ring when the -- when it got short. But she -- every once in a while you'd check for no, no good gauge to see it was -- that it was within tolerance. And if it was gettin' close, you took and stopped it, took and pulled the head and put another head on and run two or three pieces and checked it and adjust it to get it in tolerance and then away you'd go. And that was easy. And the machinery, I'd scrape the ways and if -- if I needed a gear or something like that, I'd make a pattern and I would send it down to -- down to the foundry and they'd cast me a pattern and then I'd mill -- mill a gear for it. And we put -- and they was getting 90 percent of new prices for a lathe or shaver or milling -- milling machine. And it was -- it was a lot of fun. But I worked -- then I worked Saturdays all day. And then in my senior year, I'd go to high school first thing in the morning, and I was on the wrestling team so I'd take and work out -- I'd go at 6:00 in the morning and I'd work out until 7:30, then I'd go to homeroom and I'd go to English, then I'd go to work. And that's what --

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: You were -- you were upset about Pearl Harbor when you joined the Navy and then eventually you got to Pearl Harbor not that long after the attack.

sp.speaker: Mathew William Gundersen
sp.p: Right. Oh --

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: What was your impression of the harbor?

sp.speaker: Mathew William Gundersen
sp.p: Oh, there was that much oil, an inch of oil all over everything. And battleship row, that's where we tied up. At Ford Island there, we'd tie up at Ford Island, in between the -- I forget the -- I know the Arizona was there but there was three of them in a row right there. And the West Virginia was there, one of them. I think the West Virginia is the one that was capsized. And I watched -- when they put the cables over and -- 'cause one trip they was doin' it and the next week they had it jacked up. And it was very, very interesting seeing how they put -- the California was in dry dock and they did a beautiful job on the California. Boy, she looks like she came out. But in -- in another dry dock, the Cassin and Downes were there and they burnt -- the hulls were just like corrugated tin. You've seen this corrugated tin for the roofs? Well, that's how the Cassin and Downes looked. The Downes they put back in commission again. The Cassin was too badly damaged. But it -- it was -- we'd get liberty. We'd get liberty from 1 to 4:00 liberty. And at the time it was going to Pearl Harbor. From Pearl Harbor to downtown Honolulu and then back again. And you get into town and you're allowed two beers. You couldn't buy more than two beers. It was quite aways. But you had to be back. There was many times I got a ride back with -- with the skipper. I'd miss my boat and I'd run over and get in with the gig with the skipper. Yeah, they always -- it was good.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Let's change --

sp.speaker: Mathew William Gundersen
sp.p: Thousands and thousands of caves. You know, we -- we was draw fire is what we were. And the cruises and battleship in back of us, then they'd shoot these caves, cave them in. You know, what they do is close up the caves.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, one last question about -- about the Hammondsport. Well, you went to Guadalcanal and you did that pretty early on.

sp.speaker: Mathew William Gundersen
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: I just wondered what your impressions were of Guadalcanal.

sp.speaker: Mathew William Gundersen
sp.p: Well, the -- the natives were nice and the -- the swimming pool was nice, and it -- it was good. Denver Collins: Can't hear.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Can you sit back against the --

sp.speaker: Mathew William Gundersen
sp.p: Oh, okay. Ready to go?

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mathew William Gundersen
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay, well, let's -- let's talk about coming into the shipyard and what that was like and what was going on there. Probably pretty busy place.

sp.speaker: Mathew William Gundersen
sp.p: Oh, yes. The Detroit was in there, the Ford Piper, and they were workin' on it and it was at dry dock. In fact, we had one guy in the yard there that stepped off the dock he and got killed. Got down in the Detroit. And we was -- they were building this and we was -- I forget what dry dock we were in. We were alongside the pier. They were all civilians, you know, they were doing everything. And what -- what the 12 of us were doin' was inventory and checking out things and -- but the yard was lighting off machinery and doing the finishing touch. But we checked spare parts, where they were located on the bulkheads. See, every pump had a box of spare parts. And the Navy did this on all ships until McNamara. McNamara pulled everything off the ships and -- and threw them into salvage so -- and he had two depots. McNamara just ruined the Navy by -- you have one supply depot on the east coast, Norfolk, and one supply depot in Oakland on the west coast. So if you needed a part that used to be on the spare part box on the ship, you had to go to the east coast to get it or go to the reserve fleet on one of the ships that was out of commission and get it from them. In other words, if you got a pump, you wanted a pump, you'd go to a Puget Sound reserve fleet or down to San Diego, 38 Street, reserve fleet. You'd go to order -- order a pump and they'd go down and pull it out for you and put it on your ship. But when we -- there was 12 of us and really there wasn't nothin' to do outside of inventorying spare parts and that. Because we couldn't interfere with the crew while they were installin' everything and testing it. But when it got ready for the sea trials, even the sea trials you worked with them and -- and operated the machinery but they -- they stood the watches and they did -- they had the checks on all the machinery. And our sea trial -- we had a great sea trial. We went 36 knots on our sea trial, you know, and that was -- that was -- the Leutze was an outstanding ship, had an outstanding crew and an outstanding skipper. And Robbins, Captain Robbins was a -- oh, everybody loved him. We didn't have any fear. Anytime there was -- nobody on the ship worried. And he was one of the first to get wounded on the ship to leave, you know. He got a piece of shrapnel in his neck. But he -- he recovered and he was at the -- when we put her out of commission, he was there. But in the yard we -- we -- us guys, we played -- we'd pool our nickels and dimes together and we'd go outside the gate and -- Olympia, and we'd put our money on the table and get a pitcher of beer. When the girls got off of work, they'd come out and they'd match our pot. Sometimes we'd go back to the ship with more money than we had when we started. Then we'd go the next night, you know.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: There were a lot of women working in the shipyard.

sp.speaker: Mathew William Gundersen
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Was that good?

sp.speaker: Mathew William Gundersen
sp.p: Yeah, very good. But they weren't allowed to work on the night shift. They worked day shifts. And some of them worked swing. But none of them was allowed to work graveyard. And it was -- it was -- they did a marvelous job on our ship. And, of course, we had -- we had to do the painting and stuff like that. The ships that were -- were done over at Bethlehem Steel and places, they -- they painted them completely up, the bilges and everything else, but they were in a hurry to get us gone, so they didn't -- we had to paint our own bilges and things like that. That's when we was getting a crew aboard, starting to get the crew aboard. And our first -- when we first left the yard, we took a trip -- we escorted a battlewagon to -- to Kodiak. You know, the Japanese took a -- capping _____+ they were making a faint towards Kodiak before they went into Midway. And we -- we went up there and -- but the Japanese had left, and we went up there and just made a run. Then we took -- took and escorted the carrier to Pearl and we left -- left her in Pearl and we went to -- down to the Marianas. The Marianas were taken but they'd have planes come over and drop bombs at night. But I mean, it was just -- just a look see, you know, they'd just fly over and drop a token bomb and then fly off again. And when we left there, we went down and -- and Saipan and Tyniec was already well along. And we -- we was getting a -- see, in between the two islands, the only thing we did was cruise in there and -- and draw fire. And the cruisers and the battle lines would fire above us and didn't worry about Tyniec because that was already taken care of when we got there. And in -- in the order that we went through, I -- I don't remember but we had -- like on the Hammondsport, we operated staging places, we always be at _____+. And the fleet Roses, now where Roses is down there someplace in the mine (ph), that's where -- after Midway I think it was the old Sarah was in there and she had a hole that could you drive a truck through that she was hit. And we went to Palau. I guess it was Palau first, and that's -- that's where we got the -- the captain was. We had our -- yeah, the captain was hit with shrapnel. Our number one -- we thought we were going back to the States. We went back to either Ulithi or Manus, I forget which, and we -- a week they had our stack all patched up, our uptakes all patched. They just went up and they put little patches over the shrapnel holes all through the stacks and uptakes. And we was on our way back. We escorted the -- the New York back to -- to Ulithi and -- 'cause she had -- her firing -- the New York had roll -- they had stuffing boxes on their -- on their tubes instead of roll tubes so that the vibration of them started -- started leaking. So saltwater was getting into your -- see, 'cause you carry a vacuum on your condenser. And they -- they were leaking so they went back to Ulith -- Ulithi to get that squared away. And we was right back to Peleliu?

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: What happened to the _____ that caused it? Where did the shrapnel come from?

sp.speaker: Mathew William Gundersen
sp.p: Oh, from the -- from the beach. We had to draw fire. See, now, that -- in Peleliu, that was pretty tough. There was two islands, and in between the two islands was a bridge. And every day we'd knock out that bridge and at night the Japanese would build it up. Well, we -- we'd fire flares for the Marines to shoot the people as they was comin' across the bridge or was workin' on it. And we had a marine, he was a lieutenant to begin with, we had him through all of -- I think all of our invasions. And he would go over with the Marines and he'd direct our fire. And we -- at night we illuminate it, you know, as far as -- fire illumination for the Marines. And it's just like at Guadalcanal, the Marines, they would go in and they would -- they didn't believe in sittin' down and waiting. That's -- the Army, big thing about the Army, they like to go in and put up big guns and that and sit and wait, and -- not the Marines. Like Guadalcanal, the Marines left to turn it over to the Army, the Marines had to go back in again. Because, you know, the Jap -- the one thing the Japanese were afraid of was Marines. And we -- we was at Peleliu and then Iwo Jima. And Iwo Jima was -- I forget just what -- when we was there, but we -- we had a good time there. In fact, we -- we -- that's -- that's where they -- lot of guys but we really blasted the -- right off the beach. And we had to draw fire and we was across the -- on the far side of the island, and the cruisers and that were firing into the island, because they had -- so much to hit there. The caves, it was just loaded with caves. And we went out the far side of the island to fire illumination. And, in fact, one -- one of the -- our cruisers shot a shell that exploded and it went -- went on our deck. It's just like a bunch of tin ratt -- tin cans rattling down the deck. And I had a fireman, he was on a gun watch, and it was just 7:30 in the morning when I was droppin' down in the engine room, and here come a leg right on top of me. It knocked his leg off. Burns was his name. Very fine man. Stop. Left there and -- well, we went to Leyte before then. Peleliu and Iwo Jima, we went to Leyte. And going into Leyte was the most beautiful sight I ever saw. We were on one side and Newcomb was on the other side, and the Louisville was the lead ship in. Oldendorf was part of the Louisville. And there was the cruisers and battlewagons, the carriers, and all in a line, miles of them. And we seen beautiful calm water just like glass, and we steamed into Leyte and there was no fire. And aboard our ship, because we was gonna support troops landing, we had low velocity for the beach, and so we'd go in there and -- and we hated MacArthur because he wouldn't give us any air support. And at night we'd draw patrols and we had dog Charlie, and our main engine was our main battery 'cause we -- we had all four boilers on. And a Japanese plane, about midnight they come swimmin' in with their bombs. They weren't suicide right at that time but they'd drop bombs. And, boy, we -- we'd be cruising along at five, ten knots, and we'd get -- get the word to pick up a plane and we'd kick her up. It would jump right in the water, you know, go up to 30 knots, zigzagging all over the place, you know. And none of the planes got us. There was one Jap, I -- I forget the name of it, but really that was the beginning of the suicide bombers. And that first one was really because he was hit and he just decided to go into a tin can. After about -- I don't know how many days we were there, bombs are -- every third day we used to fuel off a battlewagon. We'd get groceries, and maybe they'd give us some ice cream or something like that. And they'd -- it was pretty -- pretty nice, you know, to get some ice cream. But we -- all the -- all the new battlewagons and the carriers, Halsey took that and they was chasin' the fleet. Well, we -- we seen this Japanese fleet coming in and we -- in the afternoon, we went and got behind some islands and we just kind of cruised back and forth. And, of course, we was out of ammunition for firing at a ship and we was low on fuel. So at about 2:00 in the morning we made our first torpedo run and we made our -- made a torpedo run, laid down smoke, went out and then circled around and made another torpedo run. We made two torpedo runs. Then in the morning, because we was low -- low on fuel and we didn't have any -- any ammunition for knocking them destroyers and that out of the water, we was assigned to pick up Japanese. And they wouldn't surrender. They'd be -- have a piece of jetsam and hanging on to it, they'd be shooting at us. So the guys were all fighting topside to get a gun to shoot -- pick these Japanese off. But, you know, they was swimmin' over to the island. And, of course, I was down in the engine room so I -- I missed all that. The only thing I got to do is peek out once in a while and stick my head out the hatch, which was supposed to be dogged down, but curiosity kills the cat, you know. And it was -- it was really beautiful. We did beautiful work. We did -- the battlewagons and cruisers and wounded, they didn't go anyplace. There a few that escaped but most of them we got. And we bounced between the Seventh fleet and the Fifth fleet. And we -- I guess they changed the name. It was the same ships but they changed the fleets. But it was -- it was nice. Like we'd be -- we was in Man -- well, we -- yeah, I guess it was Manus, and they'd -- they'd be a long torpedo plane, you know, he would just fly over with the whole fleet. That was on the way to Leyte. And he'd fly over and just -- just look at us, you know. And we didn't even fool with him. He didn't get that close. And we just seen him going on through. And after Leyte, then we went up to Lingayen Gulf. Now, us and the Fox -- the Leutze and the Fox were designed to sweep the harbor, so we'd go in there and a Japanese patrol craft starts heading for us, and the old man starts to make a torpedo run and decides to blow him out of the water. I mean he blew him out of the water. The -- just one gun, the gun just blew him right out of the water. Then there was two or three patrol suicide boats, we blew them out of the water too. Then the next day there was a -- a canoe would come out and there was about a dozen guys on it and they all held up their hands, you know. Boy, they were a rough crew. They were Filipinos. They had brass knucks and bolos and things. They -- they said, "We'll lead you to the Japanese." And of course when we got them on the fantail, we made them strip completely, you know, because we didn't know what they were. But then we took them over and passed them over on the battlewagon. And the battlewagon directed the landing for us. So in Lingayen Gulf, they were 25 miles on land before they found anything. About the only thing that did anything was the battlewagons was -- they could shoot. And that was the thing, they really could go. But that -- that was -- we was about two weeks in Lingayen and we left there. When we went to Okinawa -- now, I -- I don't remember the -- I'm leaving out a lot of stuff 'cause I don't remember it. But when we went to Okinawa, we -- we were initially in -- in the invasion of Okinawa but there was a -- a cruiser at Manus and we went back to the cruiser to pick up the cruiser and -- and we brought him back. But we was back the 3rd. And the 6th we got hit -- we got suicided on the 6th. The Newcomb took three of them, and we went alongside the Newcomb. And, of course, I run a fire hose from my engine room, we were shooting it down the fire room because the torpedos fell in the fire room and burned, they didn't explode, but the steam. And the guys that died were the ones that didn't have sense enough to get down in the bilges. But the guys that got down in the bilges, we played the fire hose and they crawled out, but some of them, even though they -- they were alive, they had skin that was just falling off their arm from steam burns and things like that. And they lost quite a bit. Well, they had a suicide plane came in low and it flew over the Newcomb, and we seen him comin' and we cut lines and he hit our after storeroom on the 2100 destroyer. And from my fire -- my after engine room bulkhead, it was damaged. It took number 5 gun and threw it up in the air. And on the starboard side there was about that much room that you could -- and the fantail dropped 44 inches. The only thing that kept the fantail from falling was the screws. The screws held the fantail, the steering engine on. And, of course, my bulkhead in the engine room was going like that (indicating), so I -- when it hit, my first words -- I had two pumps that you'd blink and they'd trip off the line. They didn't. Both of them work perfectly but the bulkhead was patting aways. Now, this is about 1:00 in the afternoon. I got my crew goin' and we shored up the bulkhead. Of course, we all -- every space had shoring, you know, for this. And we practiced damage control. So we shored the bulkhead. And we had -- about 8:00 at night before I got out of the engine room. And, of course, the deck was all covered with oil and sand, blood, and -- we lost quite a few guys, and it was -- and we went -- we went to Comarada (?). That's an island off Okinawa. And there was no tender in there yet, but we -- we went to work and started to shore up the bulkhead and -- so it wouldn't fall off, we braced it up. And then when a tender got in there, we went into dry dock and we stretched canvas over the dry dock, you know, where we were working. We worked 24 hours a day on it. And what we did is, first of all, we built a framing on the open spot and -- and plated it. And so that give support. Then we, one screw at a time, we -- we didn't never did the port screw, we did the starboard screw. We took and cut the strut, raised the strut up and re -- rewelded the strut, lined the shaft up, and got our propeller so we could run the forward -- the _____ + -- now, I had a fire -- a generator in my engine room and they had one forward. Both our generators worked. So when we were in Comarada, all -- all the destroyers that would come in were damaged or dead. They'd come alongside and we'd give them power and that. But, you know, we had all our pumps, all -- everything working in the spaces, so we wasn't -- the only thing we -- we had to cut the number 5 gun off, and we did that in dry dock, and put a plate over it and raise -- when we rigged it, we could -- had to rig the -- redo the strut on the -- on the rudder to get it to work. And then we -- when we left Comarada, we took and escorted some LSTs to Guam. And now from Guam, we went -- went about 8 knots going to Guam. Then from Guam, we went about 15 knots, and then when we got to Pearl and from Pearl to the States, we went 20 knots. Well, we tested everything out all in one swoop. And we got in the yard and they started repairs but the war ended and they decided to scrap it. So we stripped all the machinery off. The idea was we'd put it out in the boxcars. And they took everything off and they -- all the crew was transferred. There was only Chief _____ and myself and about six guys, you know, to supervise. The yard was doin' the -- doin' the work and we just supervised and stuff. And then we put her out of commission. And I went aboard the Topeka and left for Japan. We got in Japan, and in Japan they was just opening up the caves and the -- the Japanese were just bringing out their wares and that. And I was on shore patrol there, and we had a marine colonel, and I would -- I had the shore patrol with the Japanese police. And the French and English, especially the French, they figured they could just walk into a shop and pick up anything they wanted and walk away. They -- they thought it was spoils of war. And these poor people just broke -- they were in sad shape. 'Cause Tokyo, you'd go up to Tokyo, you'd -- all of Tokyo, you'd see nothing but banged up areas. And the only -- only thing that be there, there would be a church by itself. Now, one thing they didn't damage was the railroad. They had it planned that they needed to be able to transfer, so they didn't hit the railroad. All the railroads were still in operation. And Tokyo was the same way, it was all bombed out. What they did is in them days they checkerboarded. You know, the bombers would go in -- when I was Okinawa, these planes would be takin' off continuous. One stream takin' off and another stream comin' in, 24 hours a day. And it was kind of funny, you know, when I was in Comarada, you know, they'd yell general quarters, and all on our ship would say, the _____ + in the mess hall in five minutes. 'Cause the only ones that got really hit in Okinawa and _____ is these guys who fired at these planes and the tracers, they'd follow the tracers then get them. So it -- it was fun.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Tell me -- we're almost out of tape, so I'm curious, how did you guys feel about the kamikaze guys? I mean, it's one thing to fight somebody, it's quite another thing to fight somebody that's just trying to die.

sp.speaker: Mathew William Gundersen
sp.p: Well, all the Japanese, they would -- they were -- they were fighters and they'd fight to the end. You know. And the only thing they were afraid of is Marines. 'Cause they thought the Marines would eat 'em. That's -- that's true. You know, in Okinawa, I mean, civilians, people, and in truck (ph), people would jump off the cliffs. I mean, rather than surrender. They thought they were going to be eaten by the Marines. They really -- they were afraid of the Marines. But, you know, in 1942, Christmas we had a bunch of rangers aboard for dinner, and these guys had ears on their belt, you know, they'd cut off Japanese they killed. And they -- they were wild men. And that group of men -- that group of men would -- they would eat snakes. That was their fame. They'd catch snakes and eat them and that. And we had brought them aboard and fed them Christmas dinner. Half the crew was afraid to go in there and eat with them. I mean, they -- they were rough. Well, they -- they -- they'd send them to New Caledonia for a month, then they'd send them to Australia for a month, and the ones that were too far gone, they'd just send them back into the field, and the rest, they sent them back to the States for rehabilitation. But there were some of them so far gone that they couldn't make it. They were -- it was interesting. (End of interview)
